deep.reconstruction:
This page is the second page of Riemann's own manuscript of the 1859 Berlin Academy paper 'Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse'. Notation: Π(s-1)=Γ(s).

(1) Contour integral representation. The previous page established Γ(s)ζ(s)=∫_0^∞ x^{s-1}/(e^x-1)dx (Re s>1). It also showed that the loop integral ∫_{+∞}^{+∞}(-x)^{s-1}/(e^x-1)dx, taken positively around 0 with log(-x) real for x<0, equals (e^{-πis}-e^{πis})∫_0^∞ = -2i sin(πs)∫_0^∞. Multiplying by i gives the first formula here: 2 sin(πs) Γ(s) ζ(s) = i ∮ (-x)^{s-1}/(e^x-1) dx.

The loop integral is entire in s. Therefore this formula continues ζ to all of C. ζ is single-valued and finite except at s=1, where sin(πs)Γ(s) has no zero to cancel the nonzero loop integral. At s=-2m (m≥1) the loop integral reduces to a residue at 0 proportional to the Bernoulli number B_{2m+1}=0. Since sin(πs)Γ(s) is finite and nonzero there, ζ(-2m)=0. [Bernoulli justification mine; Riemann just asserts it.]

(2) Functional equation by residues. For Re s<0 the integrand decays on large circles, chosen to avoid the poles. So the loop can be turned into a negatively oriented contour around the complement of the cut. The only singularities there are the simple poles x=2πin, n≠0. The negative integral around x=2πin is -2πi·Res = (-2πin)^{s-1}(-2πi).

Summing over n=±1,±2,..., with (-2πin)^{s-1}=(2πn)^{s-1}(-i)^{s-1} for n>0 and (2π|n|)^{s-1} i^{s-1} for n<0, and multiplying by i (note i·(-2πi)=2π), gives
2 sin(πs)Γ(s)ζ(s) = (2π)^s Σ_{n≥1} n^{s-1}((-i)^{s-1}+i^{s-1}).
[Simplifications mine:] (-i)^{s-1}+i^{s-1} = 2cos(π(s-1)/2) = 2 sin(πs/2). The sum is ζ(1-s). Hence ζ(1-s) = 2(2π)^{-s} cos(πs/2) Γ(s) ζ(s).

Using the duplication and reflection formulas for Γ, this becomes the symmetric form: Γ(s/2)π^{-s/2}ζ(s) is invariant under s→1-s.

(3) Second proof via theta. Motivated by this symmetry, Riemann uses Γ(s/2) instead of Γ(s): ∫_0^∞ e^{-n²πx} x^{s/2-1}dx = Γ(s/2)π^{-s/2} n^{-s}. Hence, with ψ(x)=Σ_{n≥1} e^{-n²πx},
Γ(s/2)π^{-s/2}ζ(s) = ∫_0^∞ ψ(x) x^{s/2-1} dx.

Jacobi's transformation (Fundamenta Nova p.184) states 2ψ(x)+1 = x^{-1/2}(2ψ(1/x)+1). Split the integral at 1. On (0,1) write ψ(x) = x^{-1/2}ψ(1/x) + (x^{-1/2}-1)/2. This gives
∫_1^∞ ψ x^{s/2-1} + ∫_0^1 ψ(1/x) x^{(s-3)/2} dx + ½∫_0^1 (x^{(s-3)/2} - x^{s/2-1}) dx.
The elementary integral equals 1/(s-1) - 1/s = 1/(s(s-1)). Substituting x→1/x in the middle term gives ∫_1^∞ ψ(x) x^{-(1+s)/2} dx. Final result:
Γ(s/2)π^{-s/2}ζ(s) = 1/(s(s-1)) + ∫_1^∞ ψ(x)(x^{s/2-1} + x^{-(1+s)/2}) dx.
This is valid for all s and manifestly symmetric under s↔1-s.

(4) Riemann sets s=1/2+ti and defines ξ(t) = Π(s/2)(s-1)π^{-s/2}ζ(s) = (s/2)(s-1)Γ(s/2)π^{-s/2}ζ(s). This is the entire, even function used on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors. The minor gaps are standard for the published paper.
The vanishing of the contributions from large circles needs radii chosen between poles, e.g. |x|=(2N+1)π. This is not stated.
The theta computation is first valid for Re s>1 and then extends by analytic continuation; this is implicit.
The vanishing at negative even integers and finiteness away from s=1 are asserted without the residue/Bernoulli computation.

results.what: Loop (Hankel-type) contour integral giving analytic continuation of ζ(s) to all s except a pole at 1; trivial zeros at negative even integers
results.modern_name: Riemann's contour integral representation / analytic continuation of zeta

results.what: ζ(1-s)=2(2π)^{-s}cos(πs/2)Γ(s)ζ(s), equivalently Γ(s/2)π^{-s/2}ζ(s) symmetric under s→1-s
results.modern_name: Functional equation of the Riemann zeta function
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1859 (first proof); conjectured/partly verified by Euler 1749

results.what: Mellin transform of the theta series plus Jacobi inversion giving Λ(s)=1/(s(s-1))+∫_1^∞ψ(x)(x^{s/2-1}+x^{-(1+s)/2})dx
results.modern_name: Riemann's second proof of the functional equation (theta function method)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the manuscript text of Riemann's published 1859 paper. Every result on the page is famous and universally attributed to him.

transcription_corrections: Line 'Π(s/2-1)·π^{-s/2}ζ(s) = ∫ψ(x)x^{s/2-1}dx + ∫_0^1ψ(1/x)...': in the image the limits of the first integral are hard to read and may look like ∫_0^∞. Mathematically (and in the printed paper) they must be ∫_1^∞; the transcription's ∫_1^∞ is correct.

Otherwise the transcription agrees with the image and the printed text: the 'i' in front of the loop integral, '(-n·2πi)^{s-1}·(-2πi)', '((-i)^{s-1}+i^{s-1})', 'Jacobi, Fund. S. 184', and ξ(t)=Π(s/2)(s-1)π^{-s/2}ζ(s).
